evaluation.positioning_hook: A grief-stricken Catholic cop and his shattered sister hunt a crime family that murdered their household, forcing justice, vengeance, and faith into the same blood-soaked reckoning.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is immediate: family annihilation, revenge, guilt, and redemption all land in the first act and keep paying off through the finale. The Catholic framework and crime-family engine give it a clear audience lane, though the material is more adult prestige than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening massacre, the burned photo, and the reveal that Jacob and Jodie are tied to the case make the premise legible fast. The story engine is easy to explain in two sentences: a devastated brother starts killing his way through the Risaldi family while his police-officer sister tries to stop him and solve the case.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob and Jodie are both playable, with strong emotional contradiction: he is devout and murderous, she is duty-bound and grief-struck. Victor, Ethan, and Martin each carry distinct moral positions, but the script is most magnetic when it stays close to the sibling wound and the father-son pressure inside the Risaldis.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The Catholic ritual language, confession structure, and repeated prayer imagery give the thriller a clear identity beyond standard revenge-crime mechanics. The script commits to a moral argument about sin, absolution, and inherited violence in a way that feels authored rather than generic.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps escalating through raids, interrogations, betrayals, and converging confrontations, with each act pushing the characters closer to the mansion showdown. The Christmas deadline and the repeated near-collisions between Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor keep the momentum strong.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because the revenge story is filtered through Catholic guilt, police procedure, and family confession rather than pure genre mechanics. The burned-photo motif, the adoration chapel, and the final confession booth give the premise a memorable emotional signature.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific civic ecosystem: police station, church, docks, mansion, club, press room, and graveyard all feel like parts of one pressure system. The Risaldi family hierarchy, the mayor’s spin, and the church’s role in the community add texture beyond a simple crime backdrop.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: solemn Catholic ritual collides with brutal crime violence, then keeps returning to prayer, music, and confession as emotional counterpoint. The script knows exactly when to be tender, when to be operatic, and when to go hard.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the revenge plot sits a deeper story about inherited evil, spiritual survival, and whether absolution can coexist with punishment. The repeated references to stars, storms, confession, and the pure child suggest a larger thematic design that rewards attention.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The sibling bond between Jacob and Jodie is the emotional spine, while Ethan/Martin/Victor/Frankie create a volatile family system with multiple pressure points. The ensemble is strongest when those relationships collide in rooms where loyalty, shame, and authority can all be weaponized.

casting_characteristics: One child actor in a major role (Marcus)
Multiple family members with specific age ranges
Several roles require strong emotional and dialect consistency
One role requires a physically imposing male presence (Edward)

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with recurring exterior transitions
notable_requirements: Large mansion ballroom and private rooms
Club with private decks and maintenance room

technical.vfx_details: Primarily smoke, fire, burning-photo transitions, and stylized memory/vision inserts.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, blood effects, hammer kill, stabbing, fire, smoke, and practical body-impact moments.

rights_flags.detail: Come Back by The Five Stairsteps, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, O Holy Night, 500 Miles by Peter, Paul and Mary, Clair de Lune, and Good Looking by Suki Waterhouse are all specifically used.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Prestige streaming thriller / premium cable crime drama
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with festival-to-platform or streamer original potential

cost.note: The footprint is mostly contained, but the club, mansion, docks, church, and fire-heavy finale create a mid-budget production profile.

cast.note: The script needs several strong family roles, a child actor, an infant, and at least one imposing antagonist presence to land the dynamic.

location.note: It moves through multiple recurring interiors and exteriors, including a large mansion, a club, docks, church spaces, and a press-room setup.

content.note: The script includes child murder, multiple killings, blood, grief, and explicit language, which narrows the lane to mature buyers.

rights.note: Several named songs and the Celexa brand are specifically written into the script and would need clearance planning.

strengths.what_it_means: The faith language is not decorative; it gives the movie a built-in emotional engine and a recognizable thematic lane that can travel to prestige buyers. That makes it especially attractive to actors and directors who want genre material with moral weight and a clear spiritual spine.
strengths.evidence: Confession booth scenes, adoration chapel conversations, Father Michael’s sermons, Act of Contrition structure, repeated prayer imagery.

strengths.what_it_means: The role gives a performer grief, rage, restraint, and moral collapse in one package, which is exactly the kind of part that can anchor a prestige crime feature. Mid-career dramatic leads and actors looking for a transformation role will see the appeal immediately.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s therapy outburst, the alley fight with Tyler, the confession scene, and the final confrontation with Victor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jodie has a parallel lead engine.
strengths.what_it_means: She is not just the cop side of the story; she is a grieving sister with her own pressure, which gives the film a second emotional anchor and broadens casting appeal. Strong dramatic actresses who can play authority under strain will be drawn to the role.
strengths.evidence: Her police-station scenes, her confrontation with Jacob in his apartment, and her final choice to arrest Victor and reject Jacob’s vengeance.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Risaldi family is a playable villain system.
strengths.what_it_means: Victor, Martin, Ethan, Frankie, Edward, and Alicia each occupy a distinct moral and behavioral lane, which gives the project multiple casting hooks and a rich antagonist ensemble. That kind of family hierarchy is attractive to buyers because it creates memorable faces, not just one bad guy.
strengths.evidence: Victor’s ballroom discipline, Martin’s sadism, Ethan’s conscience, Frankie’s loyalty, Edward’s brutality, Alicia’s fear.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending is built for catharsis.
strengths.what_it_means: The final convergence at the mansion, the confession booth coda, and the repeated return to the family table give the movie a clean emotional landing. That makes it easier to sell as a complete feature experience rather than just a premise.
strengths.evidence: The Christmas showdown, Jacob’s confession, the final church/reconciliation sequence, and the empty-space montage.

strengths.what_it_means: Police, church, mayor, press, and prosecutors all have a stake in the story, which makes the setting feel like a living civic machine instead of a single-location revenge piece. Buyers like that because it suggests scale without requiring a giant budget.
strengths.evidence: Briefings, press conferences, docks raid, prosecution room, church vandalism, mayoral spin.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Music and prayer create a signature texture.
strengths.what_it_means: The recurring songs and hymns give the script a sonic identity that can be marketed in trailers and used to shape emotional memory. Prestige audiences and directors who care about tone will respond to that kind of authored soundscape.
strengths.evidence: Come Back, O Holy Night, 500 Miles, Clair de Lune, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, and Father Michael’s sermon cadence.

whats_special.headline: RISALDI is a prestige crime thriller with a built-in identity: a revenge story told through Catholic confession, family shame, and the machinery of a city that let monsters grow. It offers actors two major showcase leads, a vivid villain family, and a finale that lands as both bloodletting and absolution.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is a grieving, devout family man whose faith has not protected him from becoming dangerous. He carries himself like a man trying to stay decent while every scene reveals how close he is to breaking into violence, and that contradiction is the engine of the role.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea crossed with Denzel in Flight: a man whose pain is so internalized that every release feels seismic. Actors who want a prestige lead with grief, moral corrosion, and a final-act physical payoff will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late 30s to early 40s · police officer
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is a workaholic cop who treats procedure like survival and grief like something she can outrun. She is sharp, controlled, and emotionally frayed, with a sister’s love that keeps colliding with her duty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the role territory of Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs or Amy Adams in Sharp Objects: intelligence under pressure, authority under siege, and private damage leaking through discipline. Actors who want a grounded prestige lead with procedural credibility and emotional volatility will want this.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Victor is a cold patriarch who treats his sons like instruments and cruelty like doctrine. He is composed, theatrical, and terrifyingly certain that power is morality, which makes him more than a thug — he is a worldview.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Anthony Hopkins in The Father: a commanding authority figure whose intelligence makes the menace sharper. Veteran actors who want a late-career villain role with language, control, and final-act dominance will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the conscience inside a violent family, a young man who wants meaning badly enough to risk betrayal. He is soft-spoken, principled, and constantly torn between survival and moral clarity, which makes him the story’s most fragile truth-teller.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Mescal in Aftersun or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog: a quiet, emotionally exposed role where restraint is the performance. Actors looking for a breakthrough part that can pivot from vulnerability to moral courage will be drawn to him.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s theatrical sadist, a man who performs cruelty like an art form and then collapses under the weight of his father’s judgment. He is volatile, venomous, and deeply wounded, which makes him more than a brute — he is a son trying to survive humiliation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jack Gleeson in Game of Thrones or Tom Hardy in Bronson a chance to weaponize charisma and menace at once. Actors who want a scene-stealing antagonist with emotional collapse baked into the performance will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt-force instrument, a mountain of muscle who does the ugly work without needing to speak much. He reads as controlled violence, which makes him a frightening presence even in silence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Dave Bautista in Blade Runner 2049 or Michael Shannon in supporting menace mode: a physically dominant role that communicates threat before dialogue does. Character actors with imposing screen presence will want the part because it plays instantly and memorably.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 20s to early 30s · loyal enforcer
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the family’s obedient son, the one who still wants approval even while carrying out violence. He has enough conscience to hurt, but not enough freedom to stop, which gives him real tragic pull.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the emotional obedience of Michael Imperioli in The Sopranos or Shea Whigham in supporting-crime mode: loyalty, fear, and regret in the same frame. Actors who can play wounded masculinity without losing edge will respond to him.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is a woman trapped inside a violent household, carrying fear, shame, and maternal instinct at once. She is not a passive victim on the page; she is a survivor whose silence tells you how long she has been living under Victor’s rule.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Julianne Nicholson in Mare of Easttown their best material: a woman whose pain is visible even when she says very little. Character actresses who want a bruised, emotionally loaded supporting role will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the pure child inside a corrupt family, the one person Victor still frames as salvageable. He is quiet, observant, and emotionally loaded by what he sees rather than what he says.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that can carry enormous emotional weight the way Jacob Tremblay did in Room: innocence under threat, with the audience reading everything off the face. Casting directors will see a major emotional anchor if the right young actor lands it.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the story’s spiritual counterweight, a priest who speaks in plain language but carries real authority. He is compassionate without being soft, and his presence gives the film a moral vocabulary beyond law and violence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives actors the grounded wisdom of Mark Rylance in Bridge of Spies or Brendan Gleeson in a pastoral register: warmth, authority, and spiritual texture. Veteran character actors will want it because it lets them shape the movie’s conscience.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Owens
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Owens is the calm professional trying to reach a man who wants numbness more than healing. She functions as the first person to name Jacob’s pain without indulging it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of concise but meaningful supporting role that lets an actor do the grounded clarity of Ann Dowd in a few scenes. It’s a clean, credible part for a performer who can make one conversation feel consequential.

lead_characters.name: Captain Ricks
lead_characters.hook: Captain Ricks is a weary institutional voice trying to keep a city from collapsing under scandal and violence. He is not glamorous; he is the face of compromised authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that gives a seasoned actor the procedural gravitas of Jeffrey Wright or Clarke Peters in a crime drama. It’s a strong fit for someone who can make bureaucracy feel human.

lead_characters.name: Chief Pitts
lead_characters.hook: Chief Pitts is a public-facing authority figure who understands the optics of catastrophe and the human cost underneath it. He carries the burden of leadership in scenes that need both empathy and command.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play the institutional conscience of the movie, similar to the grounded authority of John Carroll Lynch in crime material. It gives a performer a chance to be both pragmatic and emotionally legible.

lead_characters.name: Mayor Adams
lead_characters.hook: Mayor Adams is the polished public face of denial, the man who can turn catastrophe into a speech. He is smooth, evasive, and politically fluent, which makes him a useful antagonist of a different kind.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the slippery authority of a political operator in a prestige drama, like the public-facing menace of a David Strathairn type. It’s a strong fit for someone who can make spin feel dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Officer Daniels
lead_characters.hook: Officer Daniels is the practical cop who sees Jodie’s pain and keeps trying to pull her back from the edge. He functions as a grounded witness and a pressure valve in the police world.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actor the lived-in realism of a good crime-drama partner, similar to the steady presence of Shea Whigham or Michael Kelly. It’s a useful, playable part for someone who can make one line feel like history.

lead_characters.name: Xavier Winters
lead_characters.hook: Xavier is the quiet husband who has lived beside Lucy’s trauma and learned how to hold a room without taking it over. He is gentle, observant, and emotionally useful in a story that needs ordinary decency around extraordinary horror.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play the supportive, emotionally intelligent partner seen in prestige domestic drama. It’s a clean fit for someone who can make kindness feel active rather than decorative.

lead_characters.name: Lucy Winters
lead_characters.hook: Lucy is a survivor whose calm surface barely contains what she has endured. She is brave in a way that feels lived-in, not performative, and her testimony gives the movie one of its most devastating human turns.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a survivor role like the one Brie Larson had in Room or the emotional testimony space of a prestige limited-series lead. Actors who want a single-scene emotional detonation with real dignity will chase it.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a crime thriller with spiritual architecture, not just plot mechanics.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie filmmakers with at least one or two features, or TV directors moving into features, who already work well with performance-forward material and controlled violence. The sweet spot is a director who likes moral tension, ritual, and family confrontation more than spectacle for its own sake.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards precise blocking, tonal discipline, and the ability to make confession, prayer, and family dinner feel as charged as a shootout. It will attract directors who want to build a prestige calling card around actors, atmosphere, and a clear moral spine.

buyer_appeal.lane: Prestige streamer thriller / premium cable crime feature
buyer_appeal.detail: The script can be packaged around two strong lead performances and a contained recurring world, so it does not require tentpole-level scale to work. The Catholic-crime lane and the built-in Christmas setting give it a clean marketing hook for streamers and festival-to-platform buyers.

considerations.area: The opening is doing a lot at once.
considerations.detail: The massacre, the family introductions, the singing, and the time-jump all arrive in a very compressed stretch. One lever would be to let the emotional spine of Jacob and Jodie land a beat earlier so the audience has a cleaner handhold before the first major violence turn.

considerations.area: The Risaldi family map is dense.
considerations.detail: Victor, Alicia, Martin, Edward, Frankie, Ethan, and Marcus all matter, which is part of the appeal, but the family hierarchy asks the audience to track a lot of names and loyalties quickly. A next pass could sharpen each brother’s function in one defining behavior so the ensemble reads even faster.

considerations.area: The faith language is a major asset.
considerations.detail: The church scenes, confessional structure, and sermon passages are a signature, and they give the movie its identity. The version of the script where the spiritual vocabulary is even more tightly tied to Jacob’s choices would make the climax feel even more inevitable.

considerations.area: The production footprint is mid-budget, not tiny.
considerations.detail: The mansion, club, docks, church, press room, graveyard, and multiple police spaces create a real but manageable footprint. A simplification lever would be to see whether one or two of the police/press beats could share a location without losing the institutional pressure.

considerations.area: Several named songs need clearance planning.
considerations.detail: Come Back, O Holy Night, 500 Miles, Clair de Lune, and Good Looking are all specifically written into the script. If any of them are meant to be essential to the emotional architecture, that should be protected early in packaging.

considerations.area: The child roles carry emotional weight.
considerations.detail: Marcus and Jay are not decorative; they are part of the movie’s moral center and its most painful turns. The version of the production that locks those performances early will protect the emotional payoff of the family story.
